news.title: Sox postseason run has instilled pride in the South Side
news.text:
Sometimes baseball has no idea of the power it can wield. How it can ofttimes, depending on the circumstances that surround it, transcend a loss or a win, even one 21 years in the making.

“Sport has the power to change the world,” Nelson Mandela once said. “Sport can create hope where there was once only despair.”

Welcome to October. Welcome to the South Side, where despair has finally come to die.

Two seasons ago, the White Sox represented the bottomless and bottom-feeding “pit” of major-league baseball.

Today they come from a different place. Still the same side of town. Being in the American League Division Series, light-years ahead of anyone’s unrealistic thoughts, can do that to a community.

There’s the “know everything’s” claim that this is elation. That what skipper Will Venable likes to refer to as the “spirit of the team” belongs only to them. Thinking, possibly, that Munetaka Murakami’s champaign-soaked postgame meme-fest speaks only to the feeling of the team, short-sighting how an entire side of the third-largest city in America is drunk with him in that joy.

Not realizing what that team just accomplished exceeds way past baseball.

From inside Grandstand to outside on the street-level deck of Turtle’s. This ain’t just specific to 35th & Shields. This is how for a day — or seven — the people and patients walking about the Victory Center in Roseland can smile and how the kids in Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Paideia Academy in South Shore, until at least Wednesday night, can be infected with pride.

A feeling seeping inside Han Cha and Yunomi in the Stony Island Arts Bank to creeping outside Pressbox in Printer’s Row. In those eating dinner on a rainy Thursday in Ken’s on Western in Evergreen Park and getting an Italian beef or Nacho Supreme at the EZ Market outside O Block.

The Sox playing World Series-seeking baseball in October for the first time since they snatched the crown in 2005 to rewrite Chicago baseball history (a reminder: 11 years before the Cubs finally decided to shed their self-accepted “lovable losers” identity) is, as this newspaper put it, “what you don’t see in the box score.” Where we “understand how the Sox got here, what changed along the way and what the moment means to the people living it.”

It don’t rain in Southern California, but it rains bullets in the southern region of the Chi. Annie don’t live here because the sun never comes out tomorrow once you get south of Soldier Field and McCormick Place. Black being the Sox’ primary hex color because it goes with the funeral outfits so many of us on the South Side wear as customary uniforms based on the amount of services people believe we attend.

Antawun Carter and Jalil Sumerset are young diehard South Side residents and baseball savants who are finding ways to get tickets to the game Wednesday to be inside the Rate. Chance, Barack and Don C. searching their closets for postseason Sox pieces with tags still on them that they’ve been saving for just this moment. The Pope calling New Era for a new fitted.

It’s a hero’s journey that just happened to find baseball as its guide.

The first team in major-league history to lead every inning in a multiple-game postseason series is cute. But the depth of exactly what this is and reps remains far more profound than that. This isn’t about fans; this is about feelings. Feelings specific to an entire side of the city that has been continuously painted as those who are supposed to be numb to everything because of what our lives are supposed to be like on an everyday basis.

This win, this advance to the DS, this come-up before any type of come-up was thought to be logical, this culture Venable has created has infiltrated all blocks Commercial to Western, Lake Meadows to The Gardens, 18th and Blue Island Ave. to 119th and Cicero.

A less than 1% chance in April to make the postseason is the predicted market we walk around reminding ourselves of. Blurring the lines of the Sox with the lines of our lives. Happy to be trapped in their moment. Anything for the outside world to attach us to something different. To attach something positive inside of humanity to us.

For right now, for this momentary lapse in our perceived but hard to act like it doesn’t exist South Side societal anguish, the rain — at least in our minds — stops. The sun appears, if only for a week. The black we wear to match our Sox ’47s represents flyness, not funerals.

All championship teams have spirit. But until the Sox win one or even enter into that level of conversation, the true spirit of who they are, what they mean and how their impact resonates rests and breathes throughout the neighborhoods that have shouldered their burden for decades. Knowing the weight that 121 losses carries, knowing now what it feels like to have that weight lifted.

Like a roof that ain’t the ceiling. And the sun comes out. Tomorrow.

news.title: The best movies on Netflix streaming now (October 2026)
news.text:
With a library of more than 3,500 films and a labyrinth of oddly specific categories and recommendations, finding the best movies on Netflix can be a chore.

To help you with your streaming decisions, we’ve compiled a list of some of the best movies on Netflix right now, ranging from new Netflix originals to classic films from decades past.

To further assist your nightly watching decisions, we’ve sorted our best-of list into genres, so you can immediately navigate to the best horror movies on Netflix or the best comedies on Netflix using the links below. We’ll also be adding movies that are new on Netflix to the top of the article each month.

Think our list is missing something? Email [email protected] with suggestions, whether it’s about ways to make this list more user-friendly or your personal favorite best movies on Netflix that we overlooked.

New on NetflixDrama Comedy Horror Action Documentary For Kids

Best new movies on Netflix (October 2026)

‘Call Me by Your Name’ (2017)

Runtime: 132 min.Starring: Armie Hammer, Timothée Chalamet, Michael Stuhlbarg, Amira Casar

Luca Guadagnino’s coming-of-age 2017 romance is a work of intoxicating beauty, telling the story of a summer fling between precocious teen Elio (Timothee Chalmet) and confident grad assistant Oliver (Armie Hammer), who is staying with Elio’s family at their Northern Italy villa. Watching the film will leave you with a sense of yearning — whether it’s for the sun-drenched Italian countryside, the sumptuous dinner spreads, or a summer love of years gone by. Chalamet is transcendent, but don’t sleep on Michael Stuhlbarg (“A Serious Man”) as Elio’s knowing father.

Watch “Call Me By Your Name” streaming on Netflix

‘The Equalizer’ (2014)

Runtime: 132 min.Starring: Denzel Washington, Chloe Grace Moretz, David Harbour, Bill Pullman, Melissa Leo

Denzel Washington spent his entire career never starring in a single sequel until he paired up with Antoine Fuqua for “The Equalizer” franchise, about a former black ops commander named Robert McCall (Washington) trying to live a quiet retired life in Boston. Despite his efforts, McCall is pulled back into a dark world of corrupt cops, Russian mobsters, and human trafficking after befriending a sex worker (Chloe Grace Moretz). With two sequels under his belt and a third coming soon, it’s safe to say Washington has enjoyed dishing out McCall’s brand of vigilante justice — and audiences have enjoyed watching him do it.

‘The Sixth Sense’ (1999)

Runtime: 107 min.Starring: Bruce Willis, Haley Joel Osment, Toni Collette, Olivia Williams

Even if you already know the twist ending that had everyone talking back in 1999, “The Sixth Sense” is still worth revisiting when you want a scare. As a child who sees dead people, Haley Joel Osment gives one of the best child actor performances ever, and landed a fully-deserved Oscar nomination for the role. Toni Collette, playing his concerned but uncomprehending mother, is nearly as good. And don’t forget Bruce Willis, all furrowed brows and heavy sighs, as the child psychologist trying to find answers. Director M. Night Shyamalan’s career has been a rollercoaster ever since, in part because of the impossibility of living up to the standard of this film.

Watch “The Sixth Sense” streaming on Netflix

Best movies on Netflix: Drama

‘His Three Daughters’ (2024)

Runtime: 101 min.Starring: Natasha Lyonne, Elizabeth Olsen, Carrie Coon

“His Three Daughters” is a movie that will likely hit close to home for many of a certain age. Natasha Lyonne (“Poker Face”), Elizabeth Olsen (“WandaVision”), and Carrie Coon (“The Leftovers”) play three sisters whose lives followed different paths but are now forced to make nice in a cramped Manhattan apartment while caring for their ailing father. Lyonne (the stoned slacker), Coon (the uptight, judgmental mom), and Olsen (the conflict-averse yogi) speak to each other in a way that is both strangely stilted but also rooted in elemental truth about familial bonds. Watching them spar is heartbreaking, and watching them bond is hugely affirming.

Watch “His Three Daughters” streaming on Netflix

‘The Irishman’ (2019)

Runtime: 210 min.Starring: Robert De Niro, Al Pacino, Joe Pesci, Harvey Keitel

Martin Scorsese’s 210-minute crime saga follows the life of Frank Sheeran (Robert De Niro), who goes from driving trucks to leading a union, all while “painting houses” (killing people) for the likes of mobster Russell Bufalino (Joe Pesci) and protecting the interests of infamous union boss Jimmy Hoffa (Al Pacino). Instead of simply rehashing “Goodfellas,” Martin Scorsese goes deeper and darker, examining the life of a gangster who lived the life and is contemplating what it was all for.

Watch “The Irishman” streaming on Netflix

‘The Lost Daughter’ (2021)

Runtime: 121 min.Starring: Olivia Colman, Dakota Johnson, Jessie Buckley, Paul Mescal

Based on the Elena Ferrante novel of the same name, “The Lost Daughter” is yet another masterful performance from Olivia Colman, who won a Best Actress Oscar in 2019 for “The Favourite” and could have easily won a Supporting Actress award 2020’s “The Father.” In this psychological drama from actress Maggie Gyllenhaal, Colman plays a prickly college professor on vacation in Greece who inserts herself in the lives of a young mother (Dakota Johnson) and her 3-year-old daughter. “The Lost Daughter” may have missed out on a Best Picture nomination, but it’s certainly among 2021’s best.

Watch “The Lost Daughter” streaming on Netflix

‘Maestro’ (2023)

Runtime: 129 min.Cast: Carey Mulligan, Bradley Cooper

From the moment he first steps on screen in “Maestro,” Bradley Cooper is utterly magnetic as composer Leonard Bernstein. The life of the party wherever he goes, “Lenny” quickly begins a courtship with Felicia Montealegre (Carey Mulligan), each glance and one-liner delivered like he’s starring in his own sitcom. Even after decades of marriage, Bernstein still feels like he’s putting on a performance at all times, a function of both his gargantuan ego and the massive pressure of hiding his relationships with other men. As Montealegre, Mulligan sublimely captures a woman who willingly discards her own needs to support a generational talent. When Bernstein takes the stage to conduct Gustav Mahler’s “Resurrection Symphony,” with Montealegre watching in the wings, we understand why.

Watch “Maestro” streaming on Netflix

‘May December’ (2023)

Runtime: 117 min.Cast: Natalie Portman, Julianne Moore, Charles Melton

Director Todd Haynes walks an incredible tightrope act with “May December,” mixing dark comedy, melodrama, and psychological thrills to (unofficially) tell the lurid, ripped-from-the-headlines story of Mary Kay Letourneau. Actress Elizabeth Barry (Natalie Portman) shows up at the home of long-married couple Gracie (Julianne Moore) and Joe (Charles Melton, “Riverdale”) in order to shadow Gracie for a movie based on the couple’s tabloid-worthy romance. Moore and Portman have rarely been better, and Melton is a revelation — his child-like nature both amusing and heartbreaking. Not only does Haynes plumb the fragile psyche of the couple, but he also uses Portman’s Elizabeth to show how callous the Hollywood moviemaking factory can be in the pursuit of creating entertainment out of someone’s lived experiences. Portman, as it turns out, is better at playing a self-absorbed, talentless actress than most actors are at playing “real” people.

Watch “May December” streaming on Netflix

‘The Power of the Dog’ (2021)

Runtime: 126 min.Starring: Benedict Cumberbatch, Kirsten Dunst, Jesse Plemons, Kodi Smit-McPhee

Jane Campion’s Oscar-winning Western drama centers around two ranch-owning brothers, Phil (Benedict Cumberbatch, “Dr. Strange”) and George (Jesse Plemons, “The Irishman”). When George marries innkeeper Rose (Kirsten Dunst, “Bring It On”), Phil makes life difficult for her and her son, Peter (Kodi Smit-McPhee, “The Road”). Smit-McPhee is a revelation in the role, and Campion’s film is dark, foreboding, depressing, and utterly unmissable.

Watch “The Power of the Dog” streaming on Netflix

Best movies on Netflix: Comedy

‘Eighth Grade’ (2018)

Runtime: 94 min.Starring: Elsie Fisher, Josh Hamilton, Emily Robinson, Jake Ryan

Hamilton, Mass. native Bo Burnham’s directorial debut is a strikingly honest portrayal of the anxiety that pervades many middle schooler’s daily lives, as seen through Kayla (Elsie Fisher), a 13-year-old in her final week of middle school whose peers have given her the backhanded superlative of “Most Quiet.” Though he wouldn’t outright admit it in an interview with Boston.com, Burnham’s own experiences as an awkward teen who rose to YouTube fame clearly come through in the funny, heartfelt film.

Watch “Eighth Grade” streaming on Netflix

‘Frances Ha’ (2012)

Runtime: 86 min.Starring: Greta Gerwig, Mickey Sumner, Adam Driver

Whether you’re currently a city-dwelling twentysomething or simply remember the terrifyingly infinite possibilities of that period of your life, Noah Baumbach’s comedy-drama will resonate. Frances (Baumbach’s wife, director Greta Gerwig) is eking out an existence in New York City as an aspiring dancer. When her roommate (Mickey Sumner) announces she’s moving in with her boyfriend, 27-year-old Frances loses her best friend, her apartment, and her sense of self in one fell swoop. Filmed in 2011 when Instagram was first surging in popularity, “Frances Ha” shows us how comparison is the thief of joy — and why buying a solo trip to Paris with money you don’t have won’t miraculously solve all your problems.

Watch “Frances Ha” streaming on Netflix

‘Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery’ (2022)

Runtime: 139 min.Starring: Daniel Craig, Edward Norton, Janelle Monáe, Kathryn Hahn

More madcap and funny than the 2019 original, the characters and locale of “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery” shift from an old-money New England mansion to a new-money vacation compound, with Detective Benoit Blanc (Daniel Craig of James Bond fame) as the only holdover. This mystery concerns Elon Musk-esque tech billionaire Miles Bron (Edward Norton, “Fight Club”), who invites a group of his longtime friends to his private Greek island in the midst of the pandemic. As fashion entrepreneur Birdie Jay, Kate Hudson gets the most consistent laughs throughout the film, from insisting that everyone at her raucous 200-person apartment party is “in her pod” to her pathological desire to post career-ending tweets. Norton is a winner as well, playing the kind of billionaire who cultivates a worldly image that could nevertheless be deflated by a particularly clever child, a la “The Emperor’s New Clothes.”

Watch “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery” streaming on Netflix

‘Hit Man’ (2024)

Runtime: 115 min.Starring: Glen Powell, Adria Arjona

Starring the breakout actor from Richard Linklater’s 2016 film “Everybody Wants Some!!,” “Hit Man” is loosely based on a true story about a nebbish college professor named Gary (Glen Powell) who moonlights as a faux hit man for the New Orleans Police Department. Gary, so afraid of breaking his low-stakes routine, takes the undercover duties as a chance to be someone else. When he meets an alluring woman (Adria Arjona, “Andor”) while in his hit man persona (this time a tough guy named Rod), the id and the superego (also the names of Gary’s cats) collide. Powell, who co-wrote the screenplay with Linklater, carefully modulates his performance as the line between Gary and Rod blurs — though not necessarily in a bad way. “Hit Man” is sexy, thought-provoking, and funny. And for a film about a fake hit man in over his head, it’s surprisingly grounded in reality when it comes to contemplating the nature of love, hate, and self.

Watch “Hit Man” streaming on Netflix

‘Neighbors’ (2014)

Runtime: 97 min.Starring: Seth Rogen, Rose Byrne, Zac Efron, Ike Barinholtz, Dave Franco

If you loved Seth Rogen and Ike Barinholtz in Apple TV+’s Emmy-winning comedy “The Studio,” check out the pair in this 2014 comedy, about a couple of new parents (Rogen, Rose Byrne) whose move to the suburbs inadvertently places them next door to a frat house populated by hard-partying bros played by Zac Efron and Dave Franco, among others. While Byrne and Rogen try to play nice (and recapture some of their youth at a frat party in the process), the movie quickly devolves into a no-holds-barred prank war.

Watch “Neighbors” on Netflix

‘Something’s Gotta Give’ (2003)

Runtime: 128 min.Starring: Jack Nicholson, Diane Keaton, Keanu Reeves, Frances McDormand, Amanda Peet

Nancy Meyers’s romantic comedies are always elevated by the director’s larger budgets and her keen eye for gorgeous set design (think kitchens that would make Martha Stewart jealous). In “Something’s Gotta Give,” the central performances lift the film as well, with Jack Nicholson playing a serial dater who falls in love with the mother (Diane Keaton) of his latest age-inappropriate fling (Amanda Peet).

Watch “Something’s Gotta Give” streaming on Netflix

‘Sleepless in Seattle’ (1993)

Runtime: 105 min.Starring: Tom Hanks, Meg Ryan, Bill Pullman

With the proliferation of online dating, it’s amusing to think about how Nora Ephron directed two ’90s romcoms about how absolutely wild it would be if Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan fell in love electronically. With AOL’s free email service and “You’ve Got Mail” slogan yet to debut, 1993’s “Sleepless in Seattle” instead pulled Ryan and Hanks together through the radio, with Hanks attracting suitors nationwide after a Christmas Eve broadcast about his late wife. Ephron plays the audience like a fiddle, putting Hanks and Ryan tantalizingly close to each other without connecting them for the majority of the film. The duo are so winning, however, that you’ll forgive any plot contrivances when they finally get their fairy tale ending.

Best movies on Netflix: Horror

’28 Years Later: The Bone Temple’ (2026)

Runtime: 109 min.Starring: Ralph Fiennes, Jack O’Connell, Alfie Williams, Erin Kellyman

Sony’s decision to release “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple” in theaters less than seven months after “28 Years Later” was (pardon the pun) a boneheaded move. Multiple people I talked to thought the Nia DaCosta-directed sequel — one of the best movies of 2026 so far — was a re-release of Danny Boyle’s 2025 film with a few minutes of extra footage, and the box office seemingly reflected that. Spike (Alfie Williams) has fallen in with a tracksuit-clad gang of Satanists, while Dr. Kelson (Ralph Fiennes) has begun experimenting with ways to neutralize the rage-inducing virus that animates the film’s infected zombies. Regardless of where this film ends up in the year-end rankings, a show-stopping scene from Fiennes (pictured above) will undoubtedly rank among the best on-screen moments of 2026.

Watch “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple” streaming on Netflix

‘Gerald’s Game’ (2017)

Runtime: 103 min.Cast: Carla Gugino, Bruce Greenwood

Salem native Mike Flanagan (“Midnight Mass”) helms this Stephen King adaptation in which a handcuffed woman named Jessie (Carla Gugino) must escape a remote lake house after her husband suffers a fatal heart attack. This already daunting task is made tougher when Jessie begins to hallucinate, unlocking memories of her controlling husband’s behavior and a traumatizing incident from her youth. Flanagan’s deft touch and Gugino’s gutsy performance make “Gerald’s Game” stand out as a contemporary take on the survival horror genre.

Watch “Gerald’s Game” streaming on Netflix

‘Green Room’ (2015)

Runtime: 95 min.Starring: Anton Yelchin, Imogen Poots, Alia Shawkat, Callum Turner, Patrick Stewart

Before Netflix tapped him to direct 2024’s “Rebel Ridge” (also on this list), Jeremy Saulnier first broke into the mainstream with this harrowing 2015 drama about a punk band who end up trapped in the green room of a rural Oregon bar after witnessing a neo-Nazi murder. The late Anton Yelchin (“Star Trek”) is strong in one of his final performances, but the real surprise is a chilling turn from fellow Star Trek alum Patrick Stewart as the skinheads’ coldly calculating leader.

Watch “Green Room” streaming on Netflix

‘Jaws’ (1975)

Runtime: 124 min.Starring: Roy Scheider, Robert Shaw, Richard Dreyfuss

What else is there to say about “Jaws” that hasn’t been said? The first summer blockbuster, the movie that kickstarted Steven Spielberg’s career, and the film that turned Martha’s Vineyard into a giant film set, “Jaws” still strikes fear in the hearts of audiences more than 50 years after its release. From the opening scene of a skinny dipper being devoured by the unseen monster, the tension builds on the island of Amity. By the time the unforgettable trio of aquaphobic police chief Martin Brody, precocious marine biologist Matt Hooper, and lunatic shark hunter Quint (Roy Scheider, Richard Dreyfuss, and Robert Shaw, respectively) take to the high seas to combat the beast, the suspense is almost unbearable.

Best movies on Netflix: Action

‘Godzilla Minus One’ (2023)

Runtime: 125 min.Starring: Ryunosuke Kamiki, Minami Hamabe, Yuki Yamada

Set in 1950s Tokyo, “Godzilla Minus One” follows the journey of former kamikaze pilot Koichi (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who, by failing to die at the hands of Godzilla during World War II, lives in shame and is seen as a coward. He’s part of a nontraditional nuclear family, raising an orphaned child (Minami Hamabe) with another woman who lost everyone during the war (and subsequent Godzilla rampage). When the government seeks volunteers to help stop Godzilla, Koichi sees a chance for redemption. “Godzilla Minus One” is so much more than a standard monster movie, telling a hero’s tale that doesn’t hew to Western standards while interrogating how Japanese social attitudes pre- and post-atom bomb shifted. Not to worry, though: Godzilla still smashes and roars with the best of them, and looks better than his American counterpart on a fraction of the budget.

Watch “Godzilla Minus One” streaming on Netflix

‘The Killer’ (2023)

Runtime: 119 min.Starring: Michael Fassbender, Tilda Swinton

David Fincher subverts expectations with “The Killer,” in which Michael Fassbender at first seems to be playing the prototypical contract killer. He has a set of rules, a code, and high-tech weaponry to get the job done. But even before he makes a mistake that sends him on the run, you begin to suspect that Fassbender may not be nearly as suave as his self-image. Indeed, “The Killer” posits that even elite assassins are no different than Uber drivers in a gig economy, with both of them scarfing fast food in between jobs and doing whatever is needed to get a five-star rating.

Watch “The Killer” streaming on Netflix

‘The Northman’ (2022)

Runtime: 136 min.Starring: Alexander Skarsgård, Nicole Kidman, Claes Bang, Anya Taylor-Joy, Ethan Hawke, Willem Dafoe

New Hampshire native Robert Eggers (“The Witch”) leveled up in budget and scale for his third film, about a Viking prince (Alexander Skarsgard, “True Blood”) hellbent on revenge after the murder of his father (Ethan Hawke, “Training Day”). Like “The Witch,” “The Northman” is full of mottled gray landscapes and hints of the supernatural lurking below the surface. And like 2019’s “The Lighthouse,” “The Northman” tells a tale of male ego and the inevitability of violence when men are reduced to their most primitive instincts. 

Watch “The Northman” streaming on Netflix

‘Rebel Ridge’ (2024)

Runtime: 131 min.Starring: Aaron Pierre, Don Johnson, AnnaSophia Robb

Director Jeremy Saulnier’s “Rebel Ridge,” is a tale of revenge about a man named Terry (Aaron Pierre) who has his assets seized by corrupt local police on his way to post bail for his cousin. (If you haven’t read about civil asset forfeiture before, prepare to be outraged.) Unbowed and unbroken, Terry tries to handle things the right way, but Chief Sandy Burnne (Don Johnson, “Miami Vice”) won’t let him. Pierre is a magnetic leading man with action star written all over him, and you’ll be rooting for him to burn the whole force down by the time “Rebel Ridge” barrels toward its conclusion.

 Watch “Rebel Ridge” streaming on Netflix

‘Starship Troopers’ (1997)

Runtime: 129 min.Starring: Casper Van Dien, Dina Meyer, Denise Richards, Jake Busey, Neil Patrick Harris

Paul Verhoeven movies have consistently been misunderstood in their time, perhaps none more so than this sci-fi action blockbuster that bombed at the box office in 1997. Critics claimed the film — about a group of 23rd century cadets training to invade an alien planet — glorified violence and authoritarian tendencies, somehow missing that the director of “RoboCop” and “Total Recall” might be satirizing, not endorsing unchecked fascism.

Best movies on Netflix: Documentary

‘Crip Camp: A Disability Revolution’

Runtime: 108 min.Directors: Nicole Newnham, James Lebrecht

The 1960s were a time of political revolution in America, from the protests against the Vietnam War to landmark Civil Rights demonstrations. Less remembered but equally impactful were a series of protests held by Disabled in Action (DIA), an activist group that helped push reforms for the tens of millions of Americans with disabilities. The activist spirit is captured in “Crip Camp,” a documentary about a revolutionary summer camp that exposed disabled people to the free love and rock-‘n-roll lifestyle of the decade while, more importantly, treating them like human beings. 

Watch “Crip Camp: A Disability Revolution” streaming on Netflix

‘Descendant’ (2022)

Runtime: 109 min.Director: Margaret Brown

Produced by Barack and Michelle Obama’s Higher Ground Productions, “Descendant” follows members of an Alabama community known as Africatown whose ancestors were brought to America aboard the Clotilda, the last known slave ship to illegally transport slaves to the states shortly before the Civil War in 1860. The importation of slaves had been banned by Congress in 1807. After remnants of the ship were found in 2019, the film reveals how the residents of Africatown grapple with the implications the ship’s discovery has on their heritage and knowledge of self.

‘Dick Johnson Is Dead’ (2020)

Runtime: 90 min.Director: Kirsten Johnson

Death is not an easy thing to approach, especially when it comes to those we love most. In “Dick Johnson Is Dead,” documentary filmmaker Kirsten Johnson confronts the cognitive and physical decline of her father in a darkly comic way, filming her father dying over and over again, often in hilariously macabre circumstances. While Kirsten uses stunt doubles for some of the more physically taxing deaths, her father is with her the whole way, smiling and laughing as he helps support his daughter’s vision. You’ll laugh, you’ll cry, and you’ll be reminded that everyone’s grieving process manifests itself in different ways. 

Watch “Dick Johnson Is Dead” streaming on Netflix

‘Will & Harper’ (2024)

Runtime: 114 minutesDirector: Josh Greenbaum

Will Ferrell and his longtime best friend, former “SNL” head writer Harper Steele, embark on a cross-country road trip with a dual purpose: Harper (who has recently transitioned to living as a woman) wants to find out whether she still feels comfortable in her favorite types of spaces (dive bars, sports arenas), while Will wants to support his friend and ask the kind of questions many Americans have. There are moments that feel a bit too scripted for the documentary conceit, but there are also genuinely harrowing moments of self-reflection for both Will and Harper as they crisscross the deep South. “Will & Harper” not only offers a path to understanding for Americans who know little about the lived trans experience, but reminds all of us that open and candid conversations with our friends, no matter how tough they might be, are always worth having.

Watch “Will & Harper” streaming on Netflix

Best movies on Netflix: For Kids

‘Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio’

Runtime: 114 min.Starring: Ewan McGregor, David Bradley

“Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio” is so named not only as a marketing ploy, but also because the “Shape of Water” director’s take on the classic fairy tale is so wholly his own. There are still plenty of familiar elements, from a talking cricket (though not named Jiminy) to dodgy villains who lead Pinocchio astray. But the stop-motion visuals from co-director Mark Gustafson feel like Geppetto himself hand-crafted them, and the intriguing undercurrent of fascism makes the film a relevant watch for adults as well.

 Watch “Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio” streaming on Netflix

‘The Mitchells vs. the Machines’

Runtime: 114 min.Starring: Abbi Jacobson, Danny McBride, Maya Rudolph

Originally slated to be released in theaters by Sony Pictures under the title “Connected,” “The Mitchells vs. The Machines” ended up on Netflix instead due to the pandemic. After technophobic father Rick (Danny McBride, “Pineapple Express”) breaks his daughter Katie’s (Abbi Jacobson, “Broad City”) laptop before she leaves for college, he insists on canceling her flight to school and driving across the country together in order to repair their relationship. As they go, the family unwittingly becomes humanity’s last hope when a rogue AI begins to take over the world. Featuring a gorgeous animation style that evokes Sony’s “Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse,” the film has the perfect mix of kid-friendly characters and laughs that will appeal to all ages.

Watch “The Mitchells vs. the Machines” streaming on Netflix

Note: This list contains movies available to U.S. subscribers to Netflix’s Standard or Premium plans. Viewers outside of the U.S. or subscribers to Netflix’s ad-supported Basic plan may not have access to these titles.

news.title: New map highlights which US rivers should be priorities for protection
news.text:
A new map has revealed which American rivers need the most attention and protection amid the worsening climate crisis.

Only six percent of these water bodies are currently in good condition and 14 percent need help, con-servationists and scientists said in a September study.

That’s because a century of changes to the landscape and groundwater usage have forced species that live in rivers into a rapid decline.

But by identifying these areas, the researchers say there’s already been progress to protect the rivers. Dams have been identified for removal and land has been prioritized for protection around the rivers’ sources.

“We can now point at a map for the first time and say, these are the rivers most capable of sustaining diversity of aquatic life, and this is what each one needs,” Mary Khoury, a freshwater ecologist at The Nature Conservancy, which led the study, told Science News on Wednesday.

The four-year-long analysis - which included 5.2 million miles of rivers and streams in the lower 48 - showed that a third were above-average for resilience to manmade climate change. Although these rivers may still require restoration.

These rivers are found along the Pacific Coast, the Northern Rocky Mountains, the Great Lakes areas in Wisconsin and Minnesota, in Northern Maine and in coastal regions along the southeastern U.S. and the Gulf Coast.

Vulnerable or below-average resilience river networks made up 15 percent. These were located in the Southwest deserts, lower New England, the shortgrass prairie east of the Rocky Mountains and the agricultural lands of the Midwestern states.

The rivers and their surrounding areas were rated on how connected the river network is, whether animals can freely travel through them, water quality and the condition of the land near the river, how much water it is, and how much its flows have been altered.

“A resilient system is one that gives species options and environments in which to adapt,” Khoury noted.

The team acknowledged that the maps don’t take human needs into account, but said data representing human dimensions could be combined with this analysis to identify them.

Climate change has degraded water quality in U.S. rivers due to flooding, fires, sea level rise, droughts, changes to groundwater and many other impacts, according to the non-profit National Environmental Education Foundation.

Rising temperatures can create toxic algal blooms that harm river ecosystems and lead to the spread of disease. 

Historic heat has helped Lake Mead and Lake Powell - two of America’s largest reservoirs - reach record low levels this summer. The Southwest reservoirs are offshoots of the shrinking Colorado River.

Three-quarters of rivers could lose their biodiversity due to climate change, the Nature Conservancy said in a release accompanying the research.
news.summary: Three-quarters of rivers could lose their biodiversity due to climate change, conservationists say

news.title: Turning a lens on landscapes
news.text:
Over the past few months, readers might have noticed a number of photos of the American Southwest in this magazine. We led a recent issue with a shot of the vast, tan Hansel Valley in Utah, the site of a planned data center campus. Another magazine featured sweeping vistas of Grand Staircase-Escalante, the red-rocked national monument that President Donald Trump has moved to dramatically reduce in size. And this week, our story about the dwindling water levels in Lake Powell, the country’s second-largest reservoir, shows breathtaking expanses of dry canyon plunging to a shrinking, narrow ribbon of teal green.

Staff photographer Melanie Stetson Freeman was behind the lens for all these images. She and staff writer Story Hinckley traveled together throughout the region to work on a series of environmental stories, which Mel says are among her favorites to report – in no small part because of the importance of visuals for storytelling.

“A lot of these stories we’ve been doing are about these big open lands that don’t have any human buildings or even evidence of people,” Mel told me. “You want to show the beauty of that land, which is a big part of the story.”

To illustrate scale, Mel says, she looks for objects that might give a sense of perspective – a person, a rock, or, as in her Hansel Valley cover shot, a fence line. And to find the right location for a shot, she often relies on local guides like Beth Henshaw, who in this issue brought Story and Mel to an overlook where they could capture the expanse of red rock and a “bathtub ring” that shows where the lake’s water once reached.

“Water is going to become such a huge issue for so many people,” Mel says. “This particular story of the Glen Canyon Dam and Lake Powell – it’s visually so obvious.”

That obviousness takes many forms: the challenge of water management, the pressing need for interpersonal and governmental collaboration, the opening for new solutions. Story writes about all of those in her piece this week.

What’s also obvious from Mel’s photography is the solemnity of these places and the humanity of those living and working within them.

We hope you take a moment to sit with these images.
news.summary: Over the past few months, readers might have noticed a number of photos of the American Southwest in this magazine. Staff photographer Melanie Stetson Freeman was behind the lens for all these images. She talked with me about the power of visuals for telling stories about land, nature, and stewardship.

 By FRANCINE WOLFISZ, NEWS REPORTER

A London Underground worker was seen handing out pro-Palestine stickers at a tube station - moments after a passerby claims to have heard her shouting 'Free Palestine' as she stood by the ticket barriers.
The Transport for London (TfL) staff member was caught on camera handing over a window sticker to a commuter that featured the Palestinian Authority flag entwined with the logo of the National Union of Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers (RMT).
Around the edge of the sticker were the words: 'Solidarity with the people of Palestine.'
The RMT, which represents more than 80,000 workers across the UK, actively supports the Palestine Solidarity Campaign and routinely encourages workers to take part in protest marches.
However TfL's Code of Conduct and uniform policies stipulate employees can not take part in 'political activity' while on duty, including the wearing or handing out of political material. 
As footage of the incident was shared on social media, TfL told Daily Mail it would be 'investigating the circumstances'.
Advocacy group Campaign Against Antisemitism (CAA) said the video showed 'brazen political campaigning'.
Captured at an unnamed London Underground station, a man approaches a blonde-haired female worker, wearing a blue TfL polo top, standing at the ticket barriers.

Claiming he has heard her say 'Free Palestine', he approaches her and said: 'Madam I love it. I heard two words madam that ring a bell with me - what was it? Free Palestine or something?'
Without correcting him, the woman then swiftly hands him a sticker.
'It's an RMT thing to go in your window. Do you want it?' she asks him. 
When the man asks what the RMT is, she clarifies that it is 'the train union'.
The incident comes six months after a London Underground driver was suspended after he was caught on camera saying Jews were unsafe on the Bakerloo Line while he's driving.
Attending a protest, the TfL employee was asked: 'Is it safe for Jews to ride the Bakerloo line?'
Shouting over the sound of drums and crowd chants, he callously responded: 'Not when I'm driving.'
The Tube worker could be seen at the demonstration brandishing a green banner with a red border and gold letters reading: 'National Union of Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers - Bakerloo Branch.'
The unknown London Underground employee, who wore glasses, then looked into the camera and delivered an unequivocal message to the Jewish community.
'Stay well clear,' he says. 'But you're good to go today [when he is not driving the trains].'
In another incident, a Tube driver was suspended and forced to apologise after leading a 'Free Palestine' chant on an underground train. 
Footage of the event, which took place on October 21, 2023 - just weeks after the October 7 Hamas attacks - captured the moment the driver shouted 'free free' eight times over the train's speaker system, prompting passengers to respond with 'Palestine'.
Many of the passengers travelling on the Central line are believed to have been heading to an anti-Israel march in London when the chant took place.
The driver told passengers: 'So, as I feel part of it, kindly join me as we proceed to Bond Street,' before urging for the passengers' responses to be 'louder, please, louder!'
The incident sparked fury amongst Jewish campaigners who have demanded that the unidentified driver be laid off for his 'grossly unprofessional' behavior.
British Transport Police launched a probe following public outcry over the chant, resulting in Transport for London suspending the driver.
He later wrote an apology letter passed on to Jewish groups by TfL which expressed his 'unreserved apology for any offence that may have been caused'.
Of the latest incident, CAA called on TfL to investigate any 'exclusionary behavior'.

news.title: Sydney Sweeney stuns in Baywatch-inspired swimsuit amid romantic getaway
news.text:
Sydney Sweeney proved she was a Baywatch bombshell as she enjoyed a sun-soaked getaway in Utah with her friends and her boyfriend, businessman Scooter Braun.

The 29-year-old looked incredible in a bright red one-piece swimsuit with a scoop neckline and high-cut hips, as she stood in front of a clear blue lake. The friend group traveled to Lake Powell in Utah for their vacation and did everything from hiking to wakeboarding and waterskiing together. 

Sydney included several romantic snaps with her 45-year-old boyfriend, whom she met at the wedding of billionaire Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez in 2025. 

In one photo, the Euphoria actress stood on a platform looking down lovingly at Scooter as he hugged her middle, while another picture saw her sitting on his shoulders inside a club venue.

"When your man takes you to the moon," she wrote in the caption, as her fans rushed to the comment section to share the love. 

"Reminded me of Pamela Anderson from Baywatch in the first slide," wrote one fan, while another added: "Sydney got that aura." A third chimed in: "Damn, she's perfect," while another said: "Angel human".

Sydney's sporting prowess

Sydney is a big sports fan and told Complex that she made the tough decision between pursuing acting and pursuing sports when she was younger. "I grew up loving sports. I played sports growing up. I was on a soccer team, I was on a softball team, I was on a snow ski team," she told the outlet.

"I learned how to slalom ski when I was little, and I did MMA. So sports have been a really big part of my life, and I love watching hockey and boxing, especially after playing Christie Martin. I have a really huge appreciation for every single fighter."

Learn more about Sydney and Scooter below...

"My parents always told me to fall in love with as many things as possible, so they really wanted me to try absolutely everything," Sydney continued. "I think that the idea and concept of acting was my ability and my choice to be able to not have to pick being one thing for the rest of my life."

She added: "It's broadened my world so much more than if I would've just chosen one thing…there was a moment, though, when I was 12. I really wanted to go to the X Games for wakeboarding, but that didn't happen."

A risky move

The SYRN founder has sparked controversy in recent weeks after appearing in sports betting app Novig's newest ad campaign, which saw her in her birthday suit with only sports equipment covering her.

Despite the wave of backlash, particularly from female athletes who said that Sydney's ad was reductive and sexualized women in sports, Novig reported a valuation of $2 billion in the wake of the campaign, up from $500 million.

Novig's CEO Jacob Fortinsky shared on a panel that Sydney had driven a lot of the ideas in the ad campaign, after becoming an equity partner in the company.

"It was a very exciting process to work with her both on the commercial side as well as on the creative side," he said. "It really was Sydney who was driving a lot of the visuals and the messaging."

"We're hugely supportive of women's sports," Jacob added when asked about the backlash. 

"I think it's a huge component of our platform. I think we never intended to portray female sports. Sydney's an actress, the biggest movie star in the world."

news.title: Parksville a top destination for families, Airbnb data shows
news.text:
Parksville is a top destination for Canadian families this fall, new data released by Airbnb shows.

Families are searching for “classics” such as well-known resort villages and lake towns, according to a news release by Airbnb, including Parksville.

“A Vancouver Island beach town where the tide goes out for a kilometre, with old-growth Douglas fir trails behind the sand and goats grazing on the roof at Coombs Old Country Market just up the road,” the release said.

Searches among this “classic” destination are up nearly 40 per cent year-over-year, based on Airbnb internal data on quarter two 2026 searches for Sept. 1 to Nov. 30 check-ins.

Also trending in family fall vacations are Invermere, B.C., Gravenhurst, Ont., the Blue Mountains, Ont. and Mont-Tremblant, Que.

Airbnb also looked into where Gen Z is heading out on vacation and found coastlines, escarpments and foothills are pulling these travellers toward small towns such as Colwood, B.C., Cochrane, Alta., South Bruce Peninsula, Ont., Petite-Rivière-Saint-François, Que. and Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia.

Searches for domestic stays are up 25 per cent year over year during the upcoming fall season, Airbnb said, building on a record 2025, as travellers trade city weekends for lakeside cabins and the small towns.

Rural destinations are “having a moment”, according to the release, with Haida Gwaii, Kootenay Boundary and Powell River all showing up as popular destinations in B.C.
